title: Order Number Lookup
statement: A warehouse system keeps 50,000,000 order numbers in a sorted array in memory. Each support call looks up one order number, about 2,000,000 times a day.

approaches.name: Binary search the sorted array for each lookup
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: About 26 looks per call, with no extra memory.

approaches.name: Copy every order number into a hash set
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Fast lookups, but a second copy of 50,000,000 numbers costs a lot of memory.

approaches.name: Scan the array for each call
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct, but 100 trillion comparisons a day.

approaches.name: Look at the position proportional to the number's size
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Only works when the numbers are evenly spread; otherwise it misses or falls back to scanning.

title: Slowest Printer Speed
statement: A print shop must finish 10,000 jobs of different page counts within 8 hours. The printer runs at a whole number of pages per minute, one job at a time, and the shop wants the slowest speed that still finishes in time (it saves ink).
examples: pages = [300, 1200, 500], 8 hours → the smallest speed that fits

approaches.name: Binary search the speed: check "does this speed finish in time?" in one pass
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Faster speeds always finish if a slower one does, so the answer flips once; about 30 checks of 10,000 jobs.

approaches.name: Try speeds 1, 2, 3, … until one finishes in time
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct, but the speed can be in the millions, so millions of passes.

approaches.name: Use the total pages divided by the minutes
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Ignores that jobs run one at a time with rounding, so the result can be too slow.

approaches.name: Sort the jobs by size and print the biggest first
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Order does not change the total time; it does not find the speed.

title: First Broken Release
statement: An app has 2,000,000 releases in order. A bug appeared in one release and every release after it has the bug. Testing one release takes 3 minutes. Find the first broken release.
examples: releases 1–2,000,000; release 1,384,002 is the first broken one

approaches.name: Binary search: test the middle release and keep the half that must contain the first broken one
approaches.label: best

approaches.name: Test releases one by one from the start
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct, but up to 2,000,000 tests: years of testing.

approaches.name: Test from the newest release backwards
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Still linear in the worst case.

approaches.name: Test random releases until a broken one is found
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Finds a broken release, not the first one.
